newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - More Americans listen to exotic beat of world music.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - More Americans listen to exotic beat of world music.

text.p: When Pakistani vocalist Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan performs before American audiences, he does not sing or speak a word of English and he never once moves his oversized frame from a seated position on stage.

But by the end of the show, the audience is often on its feet, some dancing in the aisles, moved by the emotion of Khan's traditional Sufi Moslem devotional music called qawwali. Some rush the stage and shower him with wads of crisp dollars, a traditional South Asian sign of appreciation.

"I loved this, it's ecstatic, it's the energy of it that just permeates your whole body," said Cathy Lynch, who clapped along with much of a recent concert in Washington. "It doesn't matter that he doesn't speak English."

Khan, whose singing has graced the soundtracks of "Dead Man Walking," "The Last Temptation of Christ" and other films, is perhaps the best known of a growing number of international musicians performing their native music in the United States to growing commercial success.

"The interest has increased really exponentially in the last few years," said Robert Browning, director of New York's World Music Institute, which sponsors concerts and recordings. As evidence, Browning and others point to an expanding number of tours and recordings by foreign artists in the United States, which has long lagged behind Europe in its appreciation for traditional music from abroad.

By offering global meditation music, Haitian voodoo chants and other world music CDs, Ellipsis Arts, a 1992-founded New York label, expects sales of $4.5 million this year, up from $3.5 million last year, owner Jeffrey Charno said.

International Music Network in Gloucester, Massachusetts, which organised just one or two world music tours a year in the late 1980s, now sponsors as many as 20 tours by groups as diverse as the Bulgarian women's choir or a group from Benin, Africa, director Anne Marie Martins said. "The whole world has really opened up in the last 10 years," she said. "But it's not an easy thing to do because you really have to do a lot of grass-roots promotion."
Some foreign musicians have gained publicity by teaming up with well-known Western names, such as Khan, who has recorded with Eddie Vedder of the rock band Pearl Jam.

Companies hope the unusual nature of their recordings will lure curious customers. For example, Shanachie Records will release this month a collaboration between a Bulgarian women's choir and the throat singers of Tuva, Russia, near Mongolia, who individually sing two and even three notes of low moans and high overtones simultaneously. "The fact that it is so off-beat is often a selling point," said Randall Grass, the company's New York general manager.
Other exotic offerings fall upon deaf ears.

A handsomely packaged collection of pygmy music from central Africa has sold just 900 copies since its October 1995 release, according to SoundScan, which tracks record sales. Another Ellipsis Arts July release of Tuvan throat singing has attracted only 100 buyers so far.

Industry experts say more successful world music albums sell 10,000 to 20,000 copies, a far cry from the million sellers of rock and pop, but a few do far better. Nusrat Fateh Ali Khan's recent "Night Song" has sold 60,000 copies, according to Real World Records. And topping the current Billboard world music charts are Spain's Gypsy Kings, whose "Best of the Gypsy Kings" has sold an impressive 383,000 U.S. copies since its March 1995 release, according to SoundScan.
Another popular genre is Celtic music.

Americans in the past have embraced others performing their native music, such as Indian sitarist Ravi Shankar in the 1960s, but experts say more foreign artists are enjoying a broader success today than ever before.

Technology explains part of the change. Small digital recorders now make it possible to journey to remote villages and tape professional-quality recordings, which is what Ellipsis Arts did to record its upcoming Haitian voodoo album.
Boredom with the usual rock 'n' roll and pop offerings has also lured music listeners to the odd timings and exotic instrumentations of indigenous music, experts say.
